input.content:
---
name: what-survives
description: >
  Answer what still stands when a requirement changes after the code was written.
  Use when a constraint arrives from outside the codebase — "we can't use X anymore",
  "legal dropped this vendor", "this library may no longer touch customer data",
  "compliance banned this dependency", "we're removing Y" — and someone needs to know
  which code breaks the new rule, what is built on top of it, and what can be left
  alone. Read-only, local, no network. The companion to what-happened: that one asks
  why code looks the way it does, this one asks what survives a rule that changed
  after it was written.
---

# what survives

A constraint landed after the work was done. Three questions follow, in this order:
which code actually violates it, what else breaks if that is ripped out, and what can
be left alone. `entire graph pivot` answers all three from the code graph and prints
the edge behind every verdict, so each claim can be checked rather than trusted.

## Build it first

`pivot` is not in the released plugin. Running `entire graph pivot` will fail with
`unknown command "pivot"`. Build the binary from this repository and call it directly —
note there is **no `graph` prefix** on the standalone binary:

```sh
go build -o ./entire-graph ./cmd/entire-graph    # needs CGO for tree-sitter
./entire-graph pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1
```

If the build fails, say so and stop. Do not fall back to grep and present the result as
if it were this analysis — the whole value here is the evidence attached to each verdict,
and grep has none.

## Run it

```sh
./entire-graph pivot --repo . --dependency <package>                       # everything
./entire-graph pivot --repo . --dependency <package> --exclude-tests --depth 1
./entire-graph pivot --repo . --dependency <package> --format plan         # for an agent
./entire-graph pivot --repo . --dependency <package> --format json         # everything, archived
```

`--dependency` takes a **package name, not a sentence**. Turning "we can't send customer
data through Library X" into `libraryx` is your job, and if the phrasing maps to more than
one package in this repo, ask which one rather than picking. An impact claim built on a
guessed target is worse than no answer.

`--exclude-tests --depth 1` is the right default for a first pass on a large repository:
it drops test files before classification rather than filtering them out afterwards, and
one hop keeps the result a shortlist a person can read in one sitting. Widen only when the
shortlist is genuinely too small to explain the problem.

## Read the verdicts

| Verdict | Means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `INVALIDATED` | this file reaches the prohibited dependency itself | must change; work these first |
| `AT-RISK` | it depends on something invalidated | recheck after the roots are fixed, not before |
| `SAFE` | parsed cleanly, no path found | leave alone |
| `UNVERIFIED` | the parser reported an error or warning on this file | **not cleared** — it was never successfully read |
| `UNREACHED` | inventory-only language, no relations parsed | unknown, not safe |

`SAFE` means no path was found in this snapshot. It is not proof that none exists. Calls
through interfaces, reflection, and generated code leave no edge to follow, so a genuinely
affected file can come back Safe. Say that out loud when reporting; do not quietly upgrade
it to "nothing else is affected".

## Read the evidence tier before acting on anything

Every evidence line is graded, because the graph knows the difference between a fact it
read and a name it matched — and before this existed, both printed identically.

```
[CONFIRMED]  evidence: IMPORTS internal/cli/verify.go -> os/exec (confidence 0.80, resolution name_only)
[HEURISTIC]  evidence: CALLS internal/cli/preflight.go -> internal/cli/verify.go (confidence 0.80, resolution package)
    VERIFY: HEURISTIC evidence — confirm in source or by test before acting on this verdict.
```

- **`CONFIRMED`** — an import declaration read from source, or a call resolved to a
  definition. Act on it.
- **`HEURISTIC`** — inferred from a name, a package, or a guessed receiver type. **Open the
  cited line and confirm the relation before you edit anything.** These are often right and
  are never proof. A real example from kubernetes: a `USES_TYPE` edge matched a *parameter*
  named `owners` to an unrelated *type* named `owners` in a different binary, in a file that
  does not import that package at all.
- **`UNVERIFIED`** — the file did not parse. The edge may be fine; what is unknown is the
  edges that are missing beside it.

Do not compare the confidence numbers. They do not separate a fact from a guess: an import
statement physically present in the source and a package-level guess both sit at 0.80.
Resolution is the axis that separates them, which is what the tier is derived from.

When a file carries a `VERIFY:` line, the verdict is not actionable on its own. Read the
source at the cited location first.

## Working the plan as an agent

`--format plan` emits `pivot-plan/v1`: one work item per classified file, ordered so that
reading it top to bottom is reading it in execution order.

Read these **before** the work items, not after — the decision about how far to trust a
plan is made before it is read:

- `known_blind_spots` — what the graph cannot see, each paired with its consequence.
- `execution_contract.must_not_claim` — what you may not assert when you are done.
- `execution_contract.must_not_do` — how this plan can be satisfied without being done.
- `validation.invariants` — the same rules as machine-checkable assertions.

Then: work `P0` before `P1`. An at-risk file cannot be verified until the root it depends on
is replaced, so fixing it first produces churn rather than progress.

Each item carries `evidence_quality` and `verification_required`. **Anything not `CONFIRMED`
requires the cited source line read, or a test run, before the item is acted on or reported
done.**

## Prove it, and do not stop at the count

Re-run the same command with the same flags and show the invalidated count reaching zero.
Then show the diff beside it:

```sh
./entire-graph pivot --repo . --dependency <package> --exclude-tests --depth 1   # count
git diff --stat                                                                  # the other half
```

**The count alone is not evidence.** `invalidated == 0` is satisfied by deleting the code
just as well as by replacing it. A healthy result looks like lines replaced rather than
removed, with no test file touched to get there — on the gorilla/mux run that was
`1 file changed, 7 insertions(+), 8 deletions(-)`, suite green before and after.

`scripts/pivot-verify.py` checks this mechanically against the plan's invariants and returns
`PASS` / `FAIL` / `PARTIAL` / `CANNOT_VERIFY`:

```sh
python3 scripts/pivot-verify.py --repo . --before-plan before.json --range HEAD~1..HEAD
```

`PARTIAL` is the normal good outcome, not a failure — whether behaviour was preserved is not
decidable from a diff. `CANNOT_VERIFY` means a check could not run; report which one and why.
It is never a pass.

## When not to use this

- The user already named the file and it is small. Read it. The graph earns its cost by
  removing exploration, and there is nothing to explore.
- The question is "why is this code like this" rather than "does it still stand". That is
  `what-happened` and `explain`, which read the checkpoint transcripts instead.
- The dependency is referred to by an alias in source rather than its canonical package
  name. Matching is path-shaped and will not resolve the alias; say so rather than
  reporting the resulting empty result as a clean bill of health.

## Never claim

- That the dependency is gone, without re-running pivot and showing the count.
- That tests pass, without having executed them and read the output.
- That `SAFE` proves no dependency path exists. It means none was found in this snapshot.
- That an `UNREACHED` or `UNVERIFIED` file is resolved. Neither was analysed.
- That a `HEURISTIC` edge is an established fact.

Right — that's a real limitation, and worth being straight about.

**Pivot models exactly one kind of constraint: a prohibited dependency.** The plan JSON even says so — `"kind": "prohibited_dependency"`.

So it handles:
- "we can't use Stripe anymore" ✅
- "this library may not touch customer data" ✅ (as "ban the library")

But it **cannot** express:
- "no background workers" — that's a pattern, not a package
- "no PII in logs" — that's a data-flow rule
- "move off REST to gRPC" — that's a migration, not a prohibition
- "this module may not call that module" — an architecture boundary

Those are all real pivots, and all out of reach today. The graph has the edges to answer some of them — `HANDLES_ROUTE`, `DATA_FLOWS`, `WRITES_FIELD` all exist — but the classifier only knows how to ask one question.

**Why it's still defensible:** the prohibited-dependency case is the most common shape a constraint actually arrives in — legal drops a vendor, compliance bans a library, a licence changes. And building one constraint kind properly, with evidence tiers and a verifier, is worth more than four kinds shallowly.

**But we shouldn't claim more than that.** If a judge asks "can it handle 'no background workers'", the answer is no, not yet — and the honest follow-up is that the constraint *kind* is the extension point: same classifier, same tiers, a different rule for what counts as a violation.

```sh
--exclude-tests     drop test files before classifying

```

Three real rules on our own repo, seconds each:

| Rule | Invalidated | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| nothing may reach `internal/sem` | **139** | 24 confirmed, 115 heuristic |
| the CLI layer may not reach the graph layer | **23** | 12 confirmed, 15 heuristic |
| `gitutil` may not shell out | **4** | 11 confirmed, 2 heuristic |

**Two things worth noticing.**

The scoping works as intended — 139 → 23 → 4 as the rule gets more specific. The 139 aren't wrong, they're just answering a question nobody asked.

**And the evidence ratio flips as you narrow.** Repo-wide, 115 of 139 are heuristic — that answer is mostly inference and you'd have to verify almost all of it. Scoped to `gitutil`, it's 11 confirmed against 2 heuristic: nearly all import declarations read straight from source. **A narrower question gets a more trustworthy answer**, and the tool now shows you that before you act on it.

Which is a nice accidental proof of the whole thesis — the tiers aren't decoration, they change how much you should trust each of those three lines.

input.content:
PivotMap

What survives when a requirement changes after the code is written.

A guide to the command, the agent skill, and the MCP server · BTW Buildathon 2026 · Track 2

Someone changes the rules after the work is done. Legal drops a vendor. Compliance bans a library. An architecture rule now forbids one part of the system from touching another. The code is already written, and somebody has to answer three questions before anyone touches anything: what actually breaks this rule, what is built on top of that, and what can be left alone?

Today that is manual archaeology. git log shows what changed but not why anyone chose it. Searching finds the banned name but not the three modules quietly built on top of it. So the work is either over-done — treating the whole area as suspect — or under-done, and something breaks in production.

PivotMap answers those three questions from a map of the codebase, and — this is the part that matters — it tells you how much of its own answer it is actually sure about.

Three doors, one engine

The same analysis is reachable three ways, because the people who need it work in different places.

For developers

The command

A terminal command. Full detail: every file, every piece of evidence, the exact line that justifies each verdict.

For coding agents

The skill

Teaches an AI coding assistant when to run the analysis and — more importantly — how much to trust each part of the answer.

For everyone else

The MCP server

Makes the analysis callable from a chat window. A product manager asks in plain English and gets a decision brief, not file paths.

The rule it answers

Every constraint PivotMap understands has the same shape:

X may no longer reach Y

That one sentence covers more than it looks like it does:

The constraintXY
"We're dropping Stripe"everythingthe Stripe library
"This library may not touch customer data"everythingthe library
"The API layer may not reach storage directly"the API layerstorage
"Nothing outside payments may use the payments internals"everything elsepayments internals

What it does not answer, and this is a real boundary rather than a missing feature: constraints about behaviour rather than dependency — "no background workers", "no personal data in logs" — and migrations, where the question is what to build rather than what breaks. Those need different analysis, not a different setting.

What the answer looks like

Every file in the codebase lands in one of five buckets:

VerdictPlain meaningWhat to do
Directly affected
INVALIDATED		 This file itself breaks the rule.Must change. Start here.
Needs validation
AT-RISK		 Breaks no rule itself, but stands on something that does. Re-check after the first group is fixed, not before.
No impact found
SAFE		 Read cleanly, and no connection found.Leave alone.
Not assessed
UNVERIFIED		 The analyzer could not read this file at all. Not cleared. Needs a human.
Not assessed
UNREACHED		 Written in a language the analyzer only inventories. Unknown, not safe.

The fourth row is the important one. Before this release, a file the analyzer had failed to read was reported as safe — "no connection found, leave alone". Five files in this project's own codebase were being reported that way while the parser was erroring on them. That is a gap in the analysis being presented as a finding about the code.

How sure is it? — the part most tools skip

A map of a codebase is built by reading the source. Some of what it finds is a fact it read directly. Some is an educated guess. Until this release, both were shown the same way.

Now every piece of evidence carries a grade:

GradeMeansWhat you should do
CONFIRMED Read straight from the source. An import statement, or a call followed to its definition. Act on it.
HEURISTIC Inferred — matched by name or by package. Often right. Never proof. Open the cited line and check before acting.
UNVERIFIED The file could not be read properly. Treat as unexamined.

Why this is not academic

Run against Kubernetes — 17,838 files of Go — the analysis produced 52 confirmed connections and 71 guesses. More of the answer was inferred than proved. One of those guesses was demonstrably wrong:

graph.go     func (n *node) setOwners(owners []OwnerReference)
                                       ^^^^^^ a variable name

prunexml.go  type owners struct
             ^^^^^^ an unrelated type, in a different program

The analyzer matched a variable called owners to a type called owners in a completely unrelated file — one the first file does not reference at all. Before this release that false connection was displayed identically to a real import statement. Now it is tagged as a guess, with a line telling the reader to check it.

This is why "no connection found" is never reported as proof that no connection exists. Some code is wired together at runtime in ways no amount of reading can see. The report says no path was found, which is a different sentence.

Door 1 — the command

# build it once (needs Go)
mise run build

# "we're dropping this library"
./entire-graph pivot --dependency github.com/stripe/stripe-go

# "the CLI layer may not reach the graph layer"
./entire-graph pivot --from internal/cli --dependency internal/sem
OptionWhat it is
--dependencyY — what may no longer be reached. Required.
--fromX — who the rule applies to. Leave out for a rule that applies everywhere.
--depth 1..5How far to follow the ripple. 1 gives a shortlist.
--exclude-testsIgnore test files.
--format planOutput a work order for an AI agent instead of a report.

Scoping matters more than it sounds. In this project, "nothing may reach the graph layer" returns 139 affected files. "The CLI layer may not reach the graph layer" returns 23. The other 116 are real, legitimate dependencies — they are simply not what the rule was about, and listing them buries the answer.

Door 2 — the agent skill

A skill is a short instruction file an AI coding assistant loads automatically when it becomes relevant. Ours fires on phrases like "we can't use X anymore" or "legal dropped this vendor".

Its value is not the commands — those are easy. It is the discipline:

  • Run the analysis first, rather than searching around and guessing.
  • Before acting on a guess, open the cited line and confirm it.
  • A file the analyzer could not read is unread, not cleared.
  • When reporting the work done, re-run the analysis and show the change alongside the number — because "zero problems remaining" is also achieved by deleting the code.

It is named what-survives, to pair with an existing Entire skill called what-happened. That one looks backward — why does this code look the way it does? This one looks forward — what still stands, now the rules have changed?

Door 3 — the MCP server, for people who don't use a terminal

MCP is a standard way for an AI assistant to call an external tool. Registering this server makes the analysis available inside a chat window — no terminal, no commands.

Why that matters: constraints usually arrive from people who cannot cost them. Legal drops a vendor; compliance bans a library; a requirement changes. Each of those people currently has to find a developer to translate the constraint into an answer.

Three of the seven tools are written for that audience, and they follow strict rules:

  • Plain language only. Never "SAFE" — a green word reads as proof to someone without the instinct to distrust it. It says "no impact found in analyzed code", and says what was not analyzed in the same breath.
  • No effort estimates. Ever. It reports shape — concentrated in one area, or spread across nine — and a decision class such as discovery required. A number of hours derived from a dependency map is false precision.
  • It refuses to guess. If "Acme Analytics" could mean three different packages, it lists them and stops. A confident, specific, wrong answer is the failure this tool exists to prevent.

What a product manager actually gets back

DECISION BRIEF
  8 places across 5 areas use this directly, with 101 further places
  needing re-checking afterwards.

SCOPE CLASS: Discovery required
  Driven by: 8 direct uses found, but 92 files were not assessed
  (31% of the analyzed set), so the picture is incomplete.
  This is a shape, not a schedule.

EVIDENCE AND CONFIDENCE
  Evidence strength      Mostly inferred. Only 23 connections were read
                         directly from source; 86 were matched by name.
  Analysis coverage      Partial. 92 files could not be assessed.
  Product interpretation Weakest of the three — confirm with an owner.

Three separate confidence statements, because a single number would hide the difference between "the evidence is weak", "we couldn't see everything", and "we're guessing which product area this maps to". Those are different problems with different fixes.

Checking the work afterwards

When an AI agent does the remediation, something has to decide whether it actually worked. That check is ordinary code, not another AI — an AI grading an AI just moves the trust problem somewhere else.

It returns one of four answers:

ResultMeans
PASSEvery check ran and passed.
FAILA check ran and did not pass.
PARTIALWhat could be checked, passed — but some things cannot be checked mechanically. This is the normal good outcome.
CANNOT VERIFYA check could not run at all. Never treated as a pass.

The reason it exists: "zero problems remaining" is satisfied just as well by deleting the code as by fixing it. Tested for real — deleting the offending file makes the original check report success, and the new checks catch it on two independent grounds.

What it cannot do

Stated plainly, because a tool that hides its limits is the thing this project exists to argue against.

  • Code wired together at runtime is invisible. Some connections are decided while the program runs, and leave nothing to read. A genuinely affected file can come back as "no impact found".
  • It does not interpret sentences. It takes a package or module name. Turning "we can't send customer data through Library X" into that name is a human or assistant step, deliberately kept outside the tool — which is what lets it run entirely offline, with no data leaving the machine.
  • Behavioural rules are out of scope. "No background workers" is not a question about what depends on what.
  • It cannot tell you how long the work will take. By design.
PivotMap is built on Entire Graph, an offline code-analysis tool. No network access, no AI model in the analysis path, no data leaves the machine. Every verdict is a rule applied to evidence that is printed alongside it, so any claim in the report can be checked rather than trusted.

what are we doing here ?

Asking: **"if we could no longer use `os/exec`, what in this repo breaks?"**

`os/exec` is Go's library for running external programs — shelling out to `git`, spawning processes.

Piece by piece:

| | |
|---|---|
| `entire graph pivot` | run the analysis |
| `--dependency os/exec` | this is the thing that's now banned |
| `--exclude-tests` | ignore test files — show me only code that ships |
| `--depth 1` | follow the ripple one step; don't chase it across the whole repo |

**The answer it gave:**

```
8 invalidated    files that use os/exec directly — must change
11 at-risk       files built on those 8 — recheck after
184 safe         read cleanly, no connection
5 unverified     the parser couldn't read these — NOT cleared
89 unreached     languages we only inventory
```

Plus the line that matters: **14 confirmed, 5 heuristic, 5 unverified** — of the evidence behind those verdicts, 14 was read straight from source and 10 needs checking.

Realistically this constraint would come from a security review — *"nothing on the request path may spawn a subprocess."* The answer is 8 files to open, not 297.
what is depth 1 mean ?

How many steps to follow the ripple outward.

```
os/exec              ← the banned thing
   ↑
git.go               ← uses it directly        = INVALIDATED
   ↑
callsite.go          ← uses git.go             = AT-RISK, depth 1
   ↑
root.go              ← uses callsite.go        = AT-RISK, depth 2
   ↑
main.go              ← uses root.go            = depth 3...
```

`--depth 1` stops after one hop: **the violators, plus whatever directly touches them.**

`--depth 2` (the default) goes one further.

**Why cap it at all:** everything eventually connects to everything. Follow it far enough and the whole repo is "at risk" — technically true, completely useless. On this repo:

- `--depth 1` → 11 at-risk
- no cap → several hundred

A shortlist you can read in one sitting beats an exhaustive list nobody opens.

**Rule of thumb:** start at 1 to see the shape. Widen only if the result looks suspiciously small.
so deptgh can be 1 to 11 - how do we decide on the depth ?

Small mix-up — **11 was the number of at-risk files**, not a depth range. Depth goes **1 to 5** (default 2).

**How to choose:**

**Start at 1.** It answers "what must I fix, and what sits directly on it." That's the shortlist a person can actually work through.

**Go to 2 when** the depth-1 answer looks too clean — you fixed the roots, and you want to know what's one step behind the things you just touched.

**Rarely beyond 2.** Each hop multiplies. On this repo:

| depth | at-risk |
|---|---|
| 1 | 11 |
| 2 | ~100 |
| unbounded | most of the repo |

By depth 3 you're not answering "what's affected," you're answering "what's in this codebase."

**The practical rule:** depth is a *reading budget*, not a correctness setting. Pick the number that gives you a list you'll actually open. If depth 1 gives you 8 files, read them. If it gives you 400, the constraint is bigger than a code change and you need a different conversation.

**One thing it doesn't do:** a deeper walk never finds *new violations*. INVALIDATED is always depth 0 — files that touch the banned thing directly. Depth only widens the "needs rechecking" ring around them.

**All 8 are imports** — every one says `IMPORTS ... -> os/exec`.

The rule is: a file is INVALIDATED if it has an `IMPORTS`, `CALLS`, or `CONSTRUCTS` edge reaching the banned thing. Here it's imports in all 8 cases, which makes sense — in Go you can't call `exec.Command` without importing `os/exec` first. The import *is* the usage.

And all 8 are **CONFIRMED** — an `import` statement is physically written in the file. That's a fact the parser read, not a guess. Nothing here needs verifying before you act on it.

The 8 files are also a coherent story, not a scatter:

- **`internal/gitutil/*`** (4 files) — the git subprocess layer
- **`internal/cli/verify.go`**, **`internal/sem/search_verify.go`** — verification, which runs commands
- **`cmd/graph-bench`**, **`internal/bench/worker.go`** — benchmark tooling

but iun general - Required remediation is due ?

**Required remediation** = files that break the rule *themselves*. Not files that depend on something broken.

A file lands there if the graph finds one of three edges reaching the banned thing:

| Edge | Means |
|---|---|
| **IMPORTS** | the file imports it — all 8 here |
| **CALLS** | it calls a function in it |
| **CONSTRUCTS** | it creates one of its types |

Those are the three ways code *touches* something directly.

**Why it's called "required":** everything else is conditional. At-risk files might be fine once you fix the roots. These can't be — the banned thing is written into them. You cannot satisfy the constraint without changing every one of these files.

That's also why it's the P0 group in the work order, and why the at-risk ring can't be verified until this group is done — you'd be testing against a foundation that's still about to change.
Production follow-up - what is this ? give me simoklar ansawer ?

**Production follow-up** = shipping code that breaks no rule itself, but stands on something that does.

They're not violations. They're **retest-after** work.

The distinction: required remediation files have the banned thing written into them — you *must* edit those. Follow-up files just call the files you're about to change. Once the foundation is swapped, they might be completely fine, or they might break because the replacement behaves differently. You can't know until the first group is done.

**Why "production":** it separates shipping code from test fallout. 100 affected test files usually collapse to "run these 3 packages." 100 affected production files is a real project. The report splits them because they're different kinds of work.

**Practically:** these are the files you re-run tests against after the P0 fix — not files you open and edit up front.

And unlike the 8 violations, these often carry `[HEURISTIC]` evidence with a `VERIFY:` line — because "A calls B" is inferred more often than "A imports B" is read.

No — **nothing has been run.** No test has failed. Nothing was executed at all.

**Test fallout** = *test files* that are affected — either they use the banned thing themselves, or they test code that does.

It's the test-file half of the same analysis. The report splits it out because 187 affected test files isn't 187 things to read — it's usually 4 commands:

**And the general rule holds everywhere here:** pivot never runs anything. It reads code and reports what it found. Whether tests actually pass is a separate step — that's what the `VERIFY:` lines and `pivot-verify` are for.

**Coverage gaps** = files the analyzer never actually checked.

Not "no problem found." **Never looked.**

Two reasons a file lands here:

- **Unsupported language** — the parser can list the file but can't read relationships in it. In your run that's 89 files: shell scripts, YAML, config, docs.

That's the difference between the two commands:

| | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| unscoped | "should anything shell out?" | 8 files — a policy audit |
| scoped | "should the graph layer shell out?" | 1 file — an architecture rule |

Both valid. Wildly different amounts of work.

**And notice the at-risk count: 3.** Those aren't necessarily in `internal/sem` — propagation isn't scoped. If `search_verify.go` has to change, anything standing on it needs rechecking regardless of which package it lives in. Scoping controls *who can violate*, not *who is affected*.

That's the design call from earlier today, and this run is what it looks like in practice.
What is os/exec?

It's Go's standard library package for **running other programs** — shelling out.

```go
import "os/exec"

exec.Command("git", "status")     // run git
exec.Command("ls", "-la")         // run ls
```

Instead of doing something inside your program, you launch a separate program and read what it prints.

**Why this repo uses it:** entire-graph talks to `git` constantly — blame, log, checkout, worktrees. Rather than reimplementing git, it runs the real `git` binary. That's `internal/gitutil`, which is 4 of the 8 files.

**Why it's a realistic thing to ban:** spawning processes is a security boundary. If any part of a command line comes from user input, you risk command injection. So a security review saying *"nothing on the request path may spawn a subprocess"* is a completely normal constraint — and exactly the kind that arrives after the code is written.

Which makes it a good demo dependency: real, widely used here, and the ban is plausible rather than contrived.
java equivalent ?

`java.lang.ProcessBuilder` / `Runtime.getRuntime().exec()`

```java
new ProcessBuilder("git", "status").start();
Runtime.getRuntime().exec("ls -la");
```

Same thing — launch an external program, read its output.

`ProcessBuilder` is the modern one; `Runtime.exec()` is the older API that still shows up in legacy code.

And it carries the same security weight — command injection through `Runtime.exec()` is a classic finding, which is why a Java shop would ban it in exactly the same way.

So if you were demoing this on a Java codebase:

```sh
entire graph pivot --dependency java.lang.ProcessBuilder --exclude-tests --depth 1
```

Though for Java you'd more often ban a third-party library — `log4j`, a payments SDK, an analytics vendor — since those are the constraints that actually arrive from legal.

Everything you've run so far is **step 1 of 3.**

```
1. PLAN      pivot --format plan     →  a work order
2. DO        an AI agent executes it →  a commit
3. CHECK     pivot-verify            →  PASS / FAIL / PARTIAL / CANNOT VERIFY
```

**Step 1** — what you've been doing. `--format plan` turns the report into a work order: one item per file, priority order, evidence attached, and a contract saying what the agent must not claim or do.

**Step 2** — a fresh agent gets *only* that plan. No prior context. It fixes the P0 items.

**Step 3** — this is the part that doesn't exist in most setups. Something has to decide whether the work actually counts. That something is **ordinary code, not another AI** — an AI grading an AI just relocates the trust problem.

**Why step 3 needs to exist at all:** you could re-run pivot, see `0 invalidated`, and call it done. But **deleting the file also gives you zero.** We tested that — `rm regexp.go`, re-run, invalidated drops to zero, and the naive check certifies the attack.

The verifier catches it on two independent grounds: the file no longer exists, and 414 lines vanished against a budget of 10.

**And the honest part:** a real, correct fix returns **PARTIAL**, not PASS. Whether behaviour was actually preserved can't be decided from a diff. A verifier that can't say *"I couldn't check this"* isn't a verifier.
